office: 22nd Judicial Circuit (City of St. Louis), Circuit Judge, Division 2: retain Judge Clinton Robert Wright?
scope_plain: Every St. Louis City voter. (St. Louis County voters decide on 21st Circuit judges instead.)
office_explainer: Trial judge for the City of St. Louis: felonies, big lawsuits, family and probate cases. Yes keeps; no removes.
why_it_matters: Yes/no question with no opponent; the judge stays if more people vote yes than no. If a judge loses, the governor picks a replacement from a nominating commission's list. The Missouri Bar's Judicial Performance Review Committee majority recommends retaining Judge Wright; it recommended retaining all 13 City of St. Louis judges on the 2026 ballot.

office: St. Louis Board of Education (St. Louis Public Schools)
scope_plain: Every St. Louis City voter: St. Louis Public Schools covers the whole city.
office_explainer: The elected board that runs St. Louis Public Schools: hires the superintendent, sets the budget and votes on plans like school closures.
why_it_matters: Two seats; you can vote for up to two. The board plans to vote Nov. 10 on the Future Ready plan, which would close schools; a newly elected member likely won't be seated in time for that vote (St. Louis Public Radio).
incumbent: Donna R. Jones and Emily Hubbard

candidates.name: Donna R. Jones
candidates.background: On the board since 2006. Lives in Walnut Park; a graduate of the district who sent her seven children to its schools. Endorsed by the teachers' union, AFT Local 420.

own_words.text: Against closing schools as laid out in the district's Future Ready plan, and against state intervention in the district or more charter schools in the city (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).
Wants more career and technical education and more financial literacy classes (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

candidates.name: Wendy Goss
candidates.background: Career educator in St. Louis Public Schools and the Ferguson-Florissant district; now works for the education nonprofit PreventEd. Lives in Princeton Heights. Endorsed by the teachers' union, AFT Local 420.

own_words.text: Would support delaying the vote on the Future Ready plan for more community input; does not support shutting down the district's magnet and gifted programs (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).
Her two priorities: helping the district regain full accreditation and building trust in it (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

candidates.name: Emily Hubbard
candidates.background: On the board since 2022, running for a second term. Lives in Carondelet; a graduate assistant at Saint Louis University finishing a Ph.D. in education policy and equity. Four children in the district.

own_words.text: Supports the Future Ready plan and says the district must close schools to spread its resources better (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).
Wants more certified teachers and better student literacy over time (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

candidates.name: Aneetra Williams Jones
candidates.background: A graduate of St. Louis Public Schools, a chaplain and founder of the nonprofit Ankh Life; her children have attended the district. Lives in St. Louis Place.

own_words.text: Does not support closing schools or winding down the magnet program as the Future Ready plan lays out (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).
Wants more career, technical and workforce programs, so more students finish school with certifications (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).

candidates.name: Zach Davis
candidates.background: Social studies teacher at Cardinal Ritter College Prep, a pastor and an adjunct professor at Harris-Stowe State University. Lives in Jeff-Vander-Lou; his granddaughter is in the district. Ran for the board in 2025 and lost. (St. Louis Public Radio spells his name Zacheriah.)

own_words.text: Would like the board to delay its vote on the school closures plan, so families have more time to see how their schools are affected (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).
Wants high academic achievement across the district and better recruiting of qualified teachers (St. Louis Public Radio's summary).
